meta.location: The land of Nephi; a forest
meta.date: ~544–420 BC (179 years after Lehi left Jerusalem)

world_behind.title: Jacob's son calls it a wrestle
world_behind.text: Verse 2 names the experience with the verb from Genesis 32, where a man wrestles with Jacob until daybreak and Jacob will not let go without a blessing. This Enos is the son of a Jacob, and his account runs all day and into the night before the voice comes. Nothing in the text points at the older story, and every element of it is present.

world_behind.title: A phrase from Ephesians
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says his father taught him in "the nurture and admonition of the Lord," which is Paul's instruction to fathers, word for word. The record uses it as a description, and it is the first thing Enos says about his upbringing.

world_behind.title: The revelation happens at work
world_behind.text: He went to hunt beasts in the forest. The prayer is not at the temple, not at an altar, and not at a set hour; it starts because words he had often heard sank in while he was doing something else. Ancient theophanies are usually located at holy places, and this one is located at a hunt.

world_behind.title: A description written by an enemy
world_behind.text: Verse 20 describes the Lamanites in the terms an enemy uses: wild, ferocious, raw meat, shaven heads, skin girdles, wandering. It comes four verses after Enos secured a covenant for their salvation, and the record leaves both in place without reconciling them.

world_behind.title: The record explains why it survives
world_behind.text: Verses 13 through 18 are the plainest statement anywhere of the plates' purpose: preserved by God's arm, brought forth at a future day, delivered to the descendants of the people who wanted them destroyed. Enos is told his fathers asked for the same thing.

words.text: He had gone out to hunt beasts, and the hunger the verse reports is not his body's. "My soul hungered" (v. 4) is the entire stated reason for the prayer: no crisis, no named sin, only an appetite. In the King James Bible the verb is plain and physical, used of Jesus fasting in the wilderness and again on the road into Jerusalem. Enos takes a word for wanting food and uses it, on a hunting trip, about his soul.

An old interjection, not an instruction to depart. "Go to" is the King James way of saying come now, or very well, and it is what the builders say to one another at Babel before they start. Here it closes the exchange: "go to, thy faith hath made thee whole" (v. 8). Its only other appearances in the record are in the allegory Jacob copied into his own book, where the lord of the vineyard uses it to send his servants out. A modern reader takes it for a dismissal. It is nearer to an all right, then.

cites.quote: go to, thy faith hath made thee whole

spans.text: go to, thy faith hath made thee whole

words.text: To visit, in this record and in the King James Bible, is to come with consequences, and the consequences run both ways. God says "I will visit thy brethren according to their diligence in keeping my commandments" (v. 10), and the same verse ends with transgressions brought down with sorrow on the offenders' own heads. One verb carries the blessing and the reckoning, and which one arrives depends on the clause attached to it. The modern sense, a friendly call, is not what is promised here.

cites.quote: I will visit thy brethren according to their diligence in keeping my commandments

spans.text: I will visit thy brethren according to their diligence in keeping my commandments

words.text: A curved single-edged blade. Its first appearance in the record is here, in a list with the bow and the ax, and it will recur eleven times, always among the weapons of this people's enemies. The word marks a distinct arms tradition.

An animal that will not turn its neck to the rein. Exodus gives the word to Israel just after the golden calf, and it stays that people's word through Deuteronomy and is still in use in Acts. Enos applies it to the Nephites without argument, as though it needed none. What he adds is harder to place: they were "a stiffnecked people, hard to understand" (v. 22). The clause can mean they were hard for their prophets to make understand, or hard for anyone to make sense of, and the verse does not settle it.

cites.quote: a stiffnecked people, hard to understand

spans.text: a stiffnecked people, hard to understand

words.text: Roughness of treatment. Enos uses it of his own generation's preaching and does not apologize for it. Nothing short of exceeding harshness and great plainness would have worked. The record's own verdict on its prophets' tone is delivered in one noun.

phrases.term: He taught me in his language, and also in the nurture and admonition of the Lord
phrases.text: Two educations, named together. A language and a way of being raised, the second in Paul's exact phrase. Everything that happens in the chapter depends on the first clause of verse 3, the words he had often heard his father speak, and this verse is where those words come from.

phrases.term: The wrestle which I had before God, before I received a remission of my sins
phrases.text: A wrestle is a contest of holds, not a conversation; the King James Bible uses the word of Jacob at Peniel and of Paul's contest against principalities, and in both the opponent is stronger and the whole question is endurance. Choosing it for prayer makes the all-day duration of verse 4 part of the definition. The sentence is also honest about sequence. The wrestle came first and the remission after, and it gives the outcome before the struggle.

phrases.term: The words... sunk deep into my heart
phrases.text: Delayed action. He had often heard them; they sank while he was hunting. The verse locates conversion in a lag between hearing and effect. That is a more patient account of how teaching works than the record usually gives.

phrases.term: And all the day long did I cry unto him; yea, and when the night came I did still raise my voice high
phrases.text: Duration made explicit, in two stages. Day, then night, and the voice raised higher rather than lower as it went on. Nothing here suggests the length was a technique. It reads as a man who could not stop, and the answer comes only after the night has come.

phrases.term: I, Enos, knew that God could not lie; wherefore, my guilt was swept away
phrases.text: To sweep is to remove by force, the way a flood or a wind clears ground. Not washed, not covered, but carried off entirely, which is why the clause needs no qualifier. And the reasoning is stated: the guilt goes because a promise was made by someone incapable of falsehood. Assurance is derived rather than experienced, and "wherefore" carries the whole verse.

Four words, and the only question in the chapter that God answers directly. Enos does not ask whether it is real; he asks by what mechanism. The answer names faith in a Christ he has never seen and who will not appear for many years.

phrases.term: I began to feel a desire for the welfare of my brethren, the Nephites
phrases.text: The first thing forgiveness produces is other people. The chapter's order makes the case: himself, then his own nation, then his enemies, in that order and without a gap. Each stage begins the moment the previous one is settled.

phrases.term: My faith began to be unshaken in the Lord; and I prayed unto him with many long strugglings for my brethren, the Lamanites
phrases.text: The hardest prayer is the last one and it takes the most work. He has already been answered twice; this one requires many long strugglings. Praying for the people who want to kill you is presented as harder than praying for your own forgiveness.

phrases.term: That the Lord God would preserve a record of my people... that it might be brought forth at some future day unto the Lamanites
phrases.text: A request that assumes his own nation's destruction. Enos asks for the record's survival on the condition that the Nephites fall. He is praying for a future in which his people are gone and their enemies are reading their book.

phrases.term: They swore in their wrath that... they would destroy our records and us, and also all the traditions of our fathers
phrases.text: The threat that makes the request necessary, and it names three targets in ascending order: the writing, the people, the memory. The record understood itself as something specifically hunted, and verse 16's covenant is the answer to this verse.

phrases.term: He covenanted with me that he would bring them forth unto the Lamanites in his own due time
phrases.text: Not a promise to protect but a covenant to deliver, with the destination specified and the timing withheld. Enos's rest in the next verse is grounded in that word, and the record's whole existence is presented here as the keeping of it.

phrases.term: Thy fathers have also required of me this thing... for their faith was like unto thine
phrases.text: He is told he is not the first. Lehi, Nephi, and his own father asked the same, and what is compared is the faith behind it. It relocates his experience from private breakthrough to family practice, and he is told this only after he has done the work.

Two words for a permanent condition, set against the chapter's whole argument that things can change. Enos had just been granted his desire concerning them, and the grant applies to a distant day. The verse is his report of the present, and it does not soften.

phrases.term: I soon go to the place of my rest, which is with my Redeemer
phrases.text: Rest is a person here, and the sentence names it twice. The last verse gathers a resurrection, a face seen with pleasure, and a room prepared, and it ends on words the book puts in God's mouth rather than in Enos's.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: The setup and the vigil
verses.text: A just father, two educations, a hunting trip, words that sink in, a hungering soul, and then prayer all day and into the night. Four verses, and the only action in them is remembering something and then not stopping.

verses.label: v. 5–8
verses.title: The answer, and the mechanism
verses.text: A voice, forgiveness, the reasoning about God's inability to lie, guilt swept away, and then the question (how is it done) answered with faith in a Christ not yet seen or come. The exchange is short and it is the only dialogue in the chapter.

verses.label: v. 9–12
verses.title: The prayer widens twice
verses.text: Forgiveness produces concern for the Nephites; that is answered with a conditional about diligence and a statement that the land is holy and cursed only for iniquity. Then the Lamanites, with many long strugglings, and a grant given because of faith.

verses.label: v. 13–18
verses.title: What he actually asked for
verses.text: The record preserved against his own people's destruction and delivered to their enemies; the enemies' oath to destroy records, people, and traditions; the promise about asking in faith; the covenant; his rest; and the information that his fathers had asked the same. Six verses, and they are the reason this book exists.

verses.label: v. 19–23
verses.title: The ministry, reported flatly
verses.text: He prophesied and testified; the Nephites tried to restore the Lamanites and failed; the Lamanites are described in an enemy's terms; the Nephites farmed and prospered; there were many prophets and a stiffnecked people; and only harshness and plainness kept them from destruction. Success and failure are given the same tone.

verses.label: v. 24–26
verses.title: The count, and the summary
verses.text: Wars in his days, a hundred and seventy-nine years since Lehi left Jerusalem, and a life described as declaring the word and rejoicing in it above the world. The dating is the only place the chapter tells the reader where it sits in the record's chronology.

verses.label: v. 27
verses.title: The last verse
verses.text: Rest with the Redeemer, mortality putting on immortality, standing before him, seeing his face with pleasure, and a sentence of welcome given in God's own voice. It is the only place in the small plates where a writer quotes what he expects to be told at the judgment.

chapter.title: The chapter is a widening
chapter.text: Himself, the Nephites, the Lamanites, and then the record itself and everyone who will ever read it. Each circle opens as soon as the previous one closes, and the last one takes the most labor. The structure is the argument about what forgiveness does.

chapter.title: Prayer is described as duration
chapter.text: All day, into the night, many long strugglings, cried continually. Nothing in the chapter reports what he said. What is recorded is how long he would not stop, which is the sense the word "wrestle" carries into the book from Genesis.

chapter.title: Assurance is reasoned
chapter.text: Verse 6 says the guilt went because God cannot lie. Enos does not report a sensation; he reports an inference from a promise. That is an unusual account of forgiveness, and that is the one the chapter chooses to give.

chapter.title: What he asks to survive is not his nation
chapter.text: Verse 13 takes the Nephites' fall as given and requests only that the writing outlast them, and outlast them for the benefit of the people who wanted it burned. He will get nothing from the answer, and neither will anyone descended from him.

chapter.title: The hostile description of the Lamanites is left standing next to the covenant for them
chapter.text: Verse 16 secures their eventual salvation; verse 20 calls them wild, ferocious, and blood-thirsty. The record does not reconcile the two, and the reader is left with a man who prayed for people whose manners he described with open distaste.

chapter.title: The book defends the tone of its own prophets
chapter.text: Verse 23 says that only the roughest possible preaching kept this people off the road to destruction, and offers no apology for it. The defense comes from a man who has just described his own conversion as beginning with words that took years to sink in.

chapter.title: A whole book in twenty-seven verses
chapter.text: The small plates compression that Jacob complained about is now total: a lifetime, a conversion, a covenant, a war record, and a farewell. Enos does not complain about the space. He fills it and stops.

applications.title: Let it take as long as it takes
applications.text: Enos prayed into the night. If something matters enough, the chapter's model is a longer prayer.

applications.title: Notice what sinks in later
applications.text: Something you heard years ago may be the thing that surfaces. Pay attention to what comes back to you while you are doing something else, and treat it as the beginning.

applications.title: Reason from the promise
applications.text: When you cannot feel forgiven, Enos's move is available: identify what was promised and who promised it, and draw the conclusion whether or not the feeling arrives.

applications.title: Widen the circle in order
applications.text: Pray for yourself, then for your own, then for the people you find hardest. Notice which stage takes the most work, because that is the diagnosis.

applications.title: Ask for something you will not see
applications.text: Enos asked for something that would only matter after his nation was gone. Name one thing worth praying for that will not benefit you at all.

applications.title: Say your father's name
applications.text: The chapter opens by crediting what he was taught. Identify one thing you were given by someone who raised you, and say so out loud to somebody.

questions.text: Have I ever wrestled about anything spiritual, or do I only ask?
What did I hear years ago that has only recently started to matter?
Do I believe I am forgiven because I feel it, or because something was promised?
When something goes right for me, how long before I think about anyone else?
Who would take me many long strugglings to pray for, and why have I not?
Whose manners do I despise while claiming to want their good?
Do I expect to see his face with pleasure, and what does my honest answer change?
